title: International Society for Ecological Economics

definition.text: The main international scholarly society for ecological economics, founded in 1989 largely on Herman Daly's work.

facts.text: It recognizes that the human economy is part of a finite biosphere and should be subject to ecological limits.
Through education, research, policy and social action it works toward an equitable and ecologically sustainable society.
Robert Costanza was its first president and the first editor of its journal.
It publishes the monthly journal Ecological Economics, launched with Elsevier in 1989, and holds regular conferences.
Herman Daly, a key founding figure, received the Right Livelihood Award in 1996 for defining a path of ecological economics.
Regional societies such as the Mesoamerican society are affiliated with it.

notes: Society summary entry: allowed one entry per society; seed of the chapter with 15 in-scope inlinks.

title: International Union for Conservation of Nature
article: International Union for Conservation of Nature

definition.text: An international organization of governments and conservation groups working on nature conservation and the sustainable use of natural resources.

facts.text: It was founded on 5 October 1948 in Fontainebleau, France, on the initiative of UNESCO and its first director general, Julian Huxley.
It produces the IUCN Red List of Threatened Species, first published as the Red Data Book in 1964, and the Red List of Ecosystems.
Its 1980 World Conservation Strategy was the first report to include a chapter on sustainable development.
Drafting that strategy led IUCN to accept that conservation by banning human presence no longer worked.
Its members agreed a definition of nature-based solutions at the 2016 World Conservation Congress.
It advises conventions such as the Convention on Biological Diversity, CITES and the UN climate convention.
Critics say it long favoured removing people from protected areas and took a mainly Northern view of conservation.
Its 2012 income was 114 million CHF, mostly from official development assistance budgets.

sources.title: International Union for Conservation of Nature

definition.text: The body that coordinates responses to environmental issues within the United Nations system.

facts.text: It was created in 1972 after the Stockholm Conference on the Human Environment and is based in Nairobi, Kenya.
Its mandate covers climate change, managing marine and land ecosystems, and green economic development.
Maurice Strong was its first head; under Mostafa Tolba it negotiated the 1987 Montreal Protocol to protect the ozone layer.
Its governing body, the UN Environment Assembly, was created in 2012 and has 193 members.
Its expert working group on biological diversity, begun in 1988, led to the draft Convention on Biological Diversity.
It administers the CITES secretariat and runs the Regional Seas Programme, set up in 1974.
Its achievements include the 2017 Minamata Convention limiting toxic mercury.
A 2020 UNEP report found that most global biodiversity efforts had failed to meet their goals.

title: World Resources Institute

definition.text: A global non-profit research organization, founded in 1982, that studies sustainable practices for business, economics, finance and governance.

facts.text: Its work centres on food, forests, water, energy, cities and climate.
With IUCN and WWF it is seen as a driving force behind environmental organizations' rising influence at the UN.
It worked with companies to develop the Greenhouse Gas Protocol, a common standard for measuring and managing emissions.
With Google Earth Engine it built Global Forest Watch, which maps forest change from Landsat satellite images.
In 1997 and 2000 it published the first comparative study of material flow accounting.
Anil Agarwal criticized a 1990 WRI emissions study as environmental colonialism, sparking debate over how national responsibility should be measured.

notes: Single NGO; included as a summary entry because sources rank it with IUCN and WWF as a leading environmental body and credit it with the GHG Protocol. Drop if the selection pass keeps only IUCN/UNEP/ISEE-level bodies.

title: Integrity Council for the Voluntary Carbon Market
article: Integrity Council for the Voluntary Carbon Market

definition.text: An independent governance body that publishes the Core Carbon Principles, criteria meant to define high-integrity carbon credits in the voluntary carbon market.

facts.text: It was set up in 2021 following the recommendations of the private-sector Taskforce on Scaling Voluntary Carbon Markets.
It assesses carbon crediting programs, judging them CCP-Eligible, and approves categories of credits that may then carry a CCP-Approved label.
In 2024 it ruled several renewable energy crediting methods ineligible for the label because of additionality concerns.
In an August 2024 test, around a third of credits did not meet its benchmark.
Critics such as Barbara Haya noted that existing programs already used ideas like additionality and permanence, yet over-crediting still happened.

contested_note: Critics doubt principle-based benchmarks can screen out over-credited projects, while supporters say they make programs more comparable.
notes: Navbox seed; kept as one summary entry for the main integrity standard-setter in voluntary carbon markets.

sources.title: Integrity Council for the Voluntary Carbon Market

title: Core Carbon Principles
article: Integrity Council for the Voluntary Carbon Market#Core Carbon Principles

definition.text: The ten principles the Integrity Council for the Voluntary Carbon Market uses as a threshold benchmark for carbon credit quality.

facts.text: They include effective governance, tracking, transparency, third-party validation and verification, additionality, permanence, robust quantification, no double counting, sustainable development safeguards and contribution to net zero.
They are grouped under governance, emissions impact and sustainable development, and applied through assessment criteria.
The full document set was published in January 2024.
They respond to concerns that credit quality is hard to judge because claimed impacts depend on counterfactual baselines and on handling leakage, non-permanence and double counting.

definition.text: A plan in which a least developed country tells the UN climate convention its most urgent and immediate needs for adapting to climate change.

facts.text: Government ministries, usually helped by development agencies, assess the country's vulnerability to climate change and extreme weather and draw up a prioritized list of adaptation projects.
NAPAs use existing information rather than original research.
Submitting a NAPA makes a country eligible for project funding from the Least Developed Countries Fund.
The fund had at least US$415 million, with US$177 million approved for 47 projects, attracting over US$550 million in co-financing.

title: Economics of Land Degradation Initiative

definition.text: A global initiative to raise awareness of the economic costs of land degradation and the benefits of sustainable land management.

facts.text: It was co-founded in 2011 by the UN Convention to Combat Desertification secretariat, Germany's development ministry and the European Commission.
It develops data and methods for valuing the economic benefits of land and land-based ecosystems for decision-makers.
It estimates the annual costs of land degradation at up to €3.4 trillion.

notes: Single initiative with 1 in-scope inlink; not central to the field. Its land-degradation cost figure may be useful to the land restoration chapter.

title: Psychological impact of climate change

definition.text: The effects climate change can have on people's mental and emotional well-being.

facts.text: Three pathways have been suggested: direct exposure to extreme weather, indirect effects such as lost income, and awareness of climate risk.
Climate change cuts farm output and deters tourism, and the resulting financial stress can lead to depression.
Using US and Mexican data, suicide rates rose by 0.7% and 3.1% respectively for a 1 °C rise in monthly average temperature.
Eco-anxiety is very rarely severe enough to need clinical treatment.

notes: Navbox seed of this chapter, but it is a concept rather than an institution; the ordering pass may move it to a climate-impacts chapter.
